paragraphs: Comparisons between deep learning architectures often highlight the best score obtained from a single trained model. This paper argues that such a score does not properly account for randomness in training. Even with the same architecture, changing the initial parameters or the order of training examples can produce different results.

The proposed alternative is a normalized expected best-out-of-n performance measure, called Boo_n. Its central idea is to evaluate the best performance one would expect from a collection of n training runs. This makes the number of opportunities to obtain a strong result an explicit part of the comparison, while accounting for variation across runs.

The contribution concerns how architecture performance is evaluated. A standout run gives an observed success, whereas an expected best-of-n quantity describes performance under a specified repeated-training setup. The paper proposes this measure to correct flaws in best-single-model reporting and make comparisons more responsive to the stochastic process that actually produces trained models.
icml-2018-a-boo-n-for-evaluating-archite.tldr: Boo_n compares architectures through normalized expected best-of-n performance, accounting for randomness across training runs.

paragraphs: This paper connects a large class of deep networks to approximation theory by expressing them as compositions of max-affine spline operators. The representation gives a mathematical way to examine the transformations inside a network. For a given input, the resulting network output can be described by an affine transformation of that input.

This view interprets classification through templates that depend on both the input signal and the class. The network compares the signal with these templates using inner products. The authors explore connections to matched-filter classification and memorization, then propose a training penalty that encourages the templates to be orthogonal. They report substantially improved classification and less overfitting without changing the network architecture.

The spline description also divides the input space into regions, providing a geometric view of how networks organize signals hierarchically. Using these partitions, the authors develop and validate a distance measure that compares signals through their partition encodings. The framework therefore supports both analysis of network behavior and concrete changes to learning and signal comparison.
icml-2018-a-spline-theory-of-deep-learni.tldr: A spline representation of deep networks reveals input-dependent templates and motivates improved training penalties and signal comparisons.

paragraphs: Adaptive sampling addresses submodular maximization when the number of selected items is limited. Its attraction is parallelism: it needs exponentially fewer sequential rounds than previously studied methods with constant-factor guarantees. These rounds measure adaptivity, because evaluations within a round can run together but later rounds depend on earlier results.

The known speed advantage comes with a theoretical guarantee of only one-third of the optimum, although experiments often produce much better solutions. This paper explains part of that gap through properties of the objective function. Under mild curvature conditions, the authors show that adaptive sampling can achieve an approximation arbitrarily close to one-half while retaining its low number of adaptive rounds.

A further result connects solution quality to a homogeneity property of the function: the approximation ratio approaches one in direct relation to that property. Experiments on real datasets allow curvature and homogeneity to be manipulated and support the predicted relationships. These findings make the guarantees more sensitive to problem structure, rather than assigning every instance the same coarse performance estimate.
icml-2018-approximation-guarantees-for-a.tldr: Curvature and homogeneity explain when adaptive sampling offers stronger approximation guarantees while preserving its parallel efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization over combinatorial structures when evaluating a candidate is expensive and the objective is available only as a black box. Two difficulties interact: the number of possible structures can grow enormously, and collecting information about their quality requires costly evaluations. An effective method therefore needs to use limited observations efficiently.

The proposed Bayesian optimization algorithm uses an adaptive, scalable model designed to identify useful combinatorial structure even with little data. The model supports the decision about which candidate to evaluate next. For this selection step, the authors introduce an acquisition function that uses semidefinite programming, making that optimization technique part of their approach to efficiency and scalability.

Experimental evaluations report that the algorithm consistently outperforms the compared methods from combinatorial optimization and Bayesian optimization. The stated result supports the combination of learning structure from scarce observations and efficiently selecting further evaluations. Its significance lies in addressing both the cost of learning about the objective and the difficulty of searching a large discrete space.
icml-2018-bayesian-optimization-of-combi.tldr: The proposed Bayesian optimization method learns combinatorial structure from scarce data and uses semidefinite programming to select evaluations efficiently.

paragraphs: Obtaining a class label for every training example can be costly or difficult when privacy is a concern. This paper introduces SU classification, a weakly supervised setting that uses two kinds of information: pairs of examples known to belong to the same class, and individual examples whose classes are unknown.

The central contribution is an unbiased estimator of classification risk constructed using only these similar pairs and unlabeled points. Risk expresses the prediction error that learning seeks to reduce. An unbiased estimator makes the weaker supervision useful for evaluating this objective, allowing the authors to formulate learning through empirical risk minimization without requiring fully labeled examples.

The authors prove that the estimation error of the resulting empirical risk minimizer reaches the optimal parametric convergence rate. This provides a statistical justification for the learning setting, alongside experiments demonstrating the method's effectiveness. The result shows how information about shared class membership can support classification even when the available supervision does not directly specify each example's class.
icml-2018-classification-from-pairwise-s.tldr: SU classification learns from same-class pairs and unlabeled examples using an unbiased risk estimator with an optimal parametric convergence rate.

paragraphs: This paper uses methods from the statistical physics of glassy systems to study how deep networks move through their loss landscapes during training. Numerical investigations across different architectures and datasets examine both the landscape's complexity and the dynamics within it. The comparison asks how far ideas about glassy behavior explain neural-network training.

The findings suggest that training slows because an increasing number of directions become flat, meaning movement along them changes the loss little. At late times, as loss approaches zero, the system diffuses near the bottom of the landscape. Although the authors observe similarities with mean-field glassy dynamics, including an absence of barrier crossing, they also identify distinctive behavior indicating different statistical landscape properties.

Underparameterized networks display more typical glassy behavior in these investigations. The contrast suggests different dynamical phases depending on whether a network is underparameterized or overparameterized. This is a numerical finding and a proposed interpretation: the paper uses the physics comparison to distinguish regimes of training behavior rather than treating all deep-network optimization as one kind of glassy process.
icml-2018-comparing-dynamics-deep-neural.tldr: Numerical comparisons suggest that flat directions slow deep-network training and that glassy behavior depends on the network's parameterization regime.

paragraphs: The Contextual Graph Markov Model is an approach to representing graph data that combines generative modeling with ideas from neural networks. Its focus is structured information: a graph's representation must account for its vertices, edges, and the context carried through their connections. The paper develops a deep architecture for learning such encodings.

The architecture is built constructively from layers of probabilistic models. These layers learn to encode graph structure incrementally, so the representation develops through successive modeling stages. Context is propagated across vertices and edges using a procedure described as efficient and scalable. This propagation is the mechanism through which connected parts of the graph contribute to the learned encoding.

The resulting representation is combined with discriminative models for structure-classification benchmarks. This connects probabilistic representation learning to the task of assigning classes to graph structures. The contribution is a layered generative approach to graph processing, with context diffusion linking local graph elements to the encodings used for classification.
icml-2018-contextual-graph-markov-model-.tldr: The Contextual Graph Markov Model builds graph encodings through probabilistic layers that propagate context for subsequent classification.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for releasing information from a database while protecting each contributor through differential privacy. The intended recipients are third parties who want to estimate population statistics. The central challenge is to provide an output that remains statistically useful without releasing the original database.

The proposed output is an estimate of the data-generating distribution's kernel mean embedding, a representation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The authors show that this representation still permits consistent estimation of a broad class of population statistics. Their release mechanism bases the embedding on entirely synthetic data points and uses the space's metric to control accuracy.

The paper describes two versions of the framework for different scenarios and proves privacy guarantees for the resulting algorithms. It also proves consistency for estimators built from their outputs, connecting the released representation to reliable population estimation as data increases. These results establish a route from private synthetic releases to statistical analysis, with the kernel embedding serving as the common mathematical object linking privacy and accuracy.
icml-2018-differentially-private-databas.tldr: Private releases based on synthetic kernel mean embeddings let third parties consistently estimate a broad class of population statistics.

paragraphs: Adam often performs well in deep learning, but its success is not consistent across problems. This paper investigates its behavior by separating two aspects of the optimizer. In the authors' interpretation, the sign of stochastic gradients determines the direction of each weight update, while an estimate of relative gradient variance determines its magnitude.

Analyzing these aspects separately helps identify which part contributes to particular behavior. The analysis extends findings about Adam's adverse effects on generalization and isolates the sign-based aspect as problematic in that analysis. This gives a more specific account of the issue than treating all of Adam's adaptation mechanisms as a single indivisible design choice.

The authors then transfer the variance-adaptation component to stochastic gradient descent, producing a new optimization method. The proposal preserves a mechanism identified within Adam while combining it with SGD. Its stated role is to expand the available options for problems where Adam fails, connecting the paper's explanation of optimizer behavior to a concrete alternative training algorithm.
icml-2018-dissecting-adam-the-sign-magni.tldr: Separating Adam's sign-based direction from variance-based step sizes motivates an SGD variant that retains variance adaptation.

paragraphs: Many Bayesian methods require approximating complicated probability distributions, including distributions with several distinct modes. This paper proposes a gradient-free variational inference method that learns Gaussian mixture approximations. It draws on stochastic search methods to fit a flexible collection of Gaussian components without relying on gradients.

The method uses information-geometric trust regions to support exploration of the sampling space and stabilize updates. A variational lower bound divides the mixture-learning objective into subproblems for the individual components and their coefficients. The number of components also changes during learning, allowing the approximation's complexity to grow toward arbitrarily accurate representations rather than fixing it in advance.

Across several tested domains, the authors report significantly better approximations than competing variational inference methods. Samples from the learned mixtures have quality comparable to samples from state-of-the-art MCMC methods that consume substantially more computational resources. These empirical findings support the combination of controlled distribution updates and adaptable mixtures as an efficient way to approximate multimodal targets.
icml-2018-efficient-gradient-free-variat.tldr: A gradient-free method uses trust regions and adaptive Gaussian mixtures to efficiently approximate complex, multimodal distributions.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximization of a sum containing both a submodular term and a supermodular term. These capture diminishing and increasing returns, respectively, and both terms are assumed nonnegative and monotone. Feasible selections obey either a size limit or p matroid independence constraints. Without additional structure, these problems admit no general approximation factor.

The authors analyze a greedy algorithm and a discrete semi-gradient algorithm using curvature measures for the two terms. They introduce a dual curvature for the supermodular component, and both measures can be computed in linear time. The resulting multiplicative guarantees depend on these curvatures and on the constraint type, identifying when efficient approximation is possible.

For a purely supermodular objective, the guarantees simplify to one minus its curvature under a size constraint, and that quantity divided by p under matroid constraints. The authors also compare their guarantees with hardness results, matching them within a constant factor and an O(log p) factor, respectively. Computational experiments support the analysis, linking practical algorithms to measurable properties of the objective.
icml-2018-greed-is-still-good-maximizing.tldr: Curvature-dependent guarantees show when greedy and semi-gradient methods can approximate constrained sums of monotone submodular and supermodular functions.

paragraphs: Generating images that are both visually convincing and diverse remains a challenge for generative adversarial networks. This paper addresses those goals by improving training stability. Its central intervention is to give the discriminator representative features learned from the data distribution, using those features as a form of implicit regularization.

A pretrained autoencoder supplies the representative features, which are transferred to a standard GAN's discriminator. The paper explains this design through two directions of Kullback-Leibler divergence. In the authors' account, standard GAN training minimizes reverse KL divergence, while the autoencoder learns through forward KL divergence. Transferring its features brings influences from both into GAN training.

Extensive evaluations report improvements in both visual quality and diversity for the evaluated state-of-the-art GANs. The result supports using an additional learned representation to shape discriminator behavior and stabilize adversarial training. The paper's proposed mechanism ties the feature transfer to complementary distribution-matching influences, connecting its training modification to the two image-generation objectives it seeks to improve.
icml-2018-improved-training-of-generativ.tldr: Transferring pretrained autoencoder features to GAN discriminators stabilizes training and improves image quality and diversity in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Representation-learning losses can remain unchanged under continuous transformations of their parameters. For example, rotating all word and context embeddings together leaves the word-embedding loss unchanged. This means different coordinate arrangements can express the same quality of solution, making symmetry relevant to the geometry of optimization.

The authors show that representation models for time series have an approximate continuous symmetry that causes gradient descent to converge slowly. They develop an optimization algorithm inspired by gauge theory in physics to address this behavior. The approach uses the symmetry structure as information for improving optimization, connecting a property of the model's parameterization to its training dynamics.

For dynamic matrix factorization and word-embedding models, the authors demonstrate convergence that is faster by orders of magnitude, together with more interpretable representations. They also present an application that translates modern words into historical equivalents. These findings show how addressing approximate symmetry can improve both computational behavior and the usefulness of representations in models that track changes over time.
icml-2018-improving-optimization-for-mod.tldr: A gauge-theory-inspired optimizer addresses approximate continuous symmetries to accelerate temporal representation learning and improve interpretability.

paragraphs: The Gaussian mechanism supports differentially private analysis by adding Gaussian noise. This paper revisits how much noise it requires. The authors show that the classical variance formula is loose when privacy is strong, as epsilon approaches zero, and that its analysis cannot extend to the low-privacy regime where epsilon becomes arbitrarily large.

They develop an optimal calibration of the Gaussian mechanism using the Gaussian cumulative distribution function directly. This avoids the tail-bound approximation used in the earlier analysis. They also add a denoising step based on adaptive estimation, taking advantage of the fact that the distribution of the added perturbation is known.

In the reported experiments, analytical calibration reduces noise variance by at least one-third relative to the classical Gaussian mechanism. Denoising produces substantial accuracy improvements in high-dimensional settings. The two changes address different stages of the same process: calibration determines the perturbation needed for privacy, while post-processing uses knowledge of that perturbation to improve the accuracy of the released result.
icml-2018-improving-the-gaussian-mechani.tldr: Direct Gaussian calibration reduces unnecessary privacy noise, while adaptive denoising improves accuracy, especially in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Tree-search methods such as branch-and-bound solve combinatorial problems by repeatedly dividing the remaining search space. At each node, choosing which variable to branch on affects the size of the resulting tree. A good branching decision therefore matters for how much search is needed to find an optimal solution.

Many procedures exist for making these decisions, but the paper notes the lack of a theory identifying which is optimal. The authors use machine learning to determine an optimal weighting of a supplied set of partitioning procedures for the distribution of problem instances at hand. Samples from that distribution provide the information used to learn the weighting.

The paper supports learning to branch through both theoretical analysis and experiments, reporting that it is practical and highly beneficial. Its central contribution is to make branching choices responsive to the kinds of instances a solver encounters. The optimality claim concerns the learned weighting for that instance distribution, tying the method's target directly to its available procedures and training samples.
icml-2018-learning-to-branch-8b9bc3a432.tldr: Learning to Branch uses samples to optimize the weighting of branching procedures for a particular distribution of combinatorial problems.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned model to reason about how a system evolves. This paper examines the role of Lipschitz continuity in such models. A Lipschitz constraint controls how much a model's output can change when its input changes, making that sensitivity a quantity that can be analyzed and regulated.

The authors derive a bound on prediction error over multiple steps, measuring error with the Wasserstein metric. This connects model regularity to the accuracy of predictions obtained by repeatedly using the model. They also prove a bound on the resulting value-function estimation error, extending the analysis from predicting system evolution to estimating its value.

A further result shows that the estimated value function is itself Lipschitz continuous. The paper therefore links regularity of the learned model with both prediction accuracy and properties of the value estimate. Empirical results demonstrate benefits from controlling the Lipschitz constant of neural-network models, supporting the practical relevance of the quantities examined in the theoretical analysis.
icml-2018-lipschitz-continuity-in-model-.tldr: Lipschitz constraints connect learned-model sensitivity to bounds on multistep prediction and value-estimation errors in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A defense can appear effective against adversarial examples because it interferes with the gradients an attack uses to search for them. This paper identifies that effect as obfuscated gradients, a form of gradient masking. The authors show that apparent resistance to iterative optimization attacks can therefore give a misleading impression of security.

They characterize the behavior of defenses exhibiting this effect and identify three types of gradient obfuscation. For each type, they develop attack techniques that overcome it. This turns the diagnosis into a practical evaluation approach: understanding why an attack struggles guides the construction of attacks that can expose the remaining vulnerability.

In a case study of non-certified defenses presented as white-box secure at ICLR 2018, seven of nine examined defenses rely on obfuscated gradients. The new attacks fully circumvent six and partially circumvent one, within each paper's original threat model. These findings show a concrete failure mode in the evaluated defenses: disrupting an attack's optimization process can conceal adversarial vulnerability without eliminating it.
icml-2018-obfuscated-gradients-give-a-fa.tldr: Obfuscated gradients can create misleading robustness claims, and tailored attacks circumvent seven examined defenses fully or partially.

paragraphs: Adding depth is often associated with greater expressive power and harder optimization. This paper investigates a different possibility: additional layers can sometimes make optimization faster. To separate this effect from expressiveness, the authors study linear neural networks, where extra layers introduce more parameters without expanding the underlying class of linear functions.

Theory and experiments show that depth can act as a preconditioner, changing the effective behavior of gradient descent in a way that may accelerate convergence. Even a convex linear-regression problem with an l_p loss for p greater than two can benefit from being rewritten as a nonconvex, overparameterized objective. In the studied settings, this benefit can exceed that of some common acceleration schemes.

The authors also prove that gradients of a regularizer cannot reproduce the acceleration effect of overparameterization. This distinguishes changing the parameterization from simply adding a penalty to the objective. The findings establish that extra depth can influence optimization favorably even when it contributes no additional expressiveness, while retaining the qualification that acceleration occurs in particular settings.
icml-2018-on-the-optimization-of-deep-ne.tldr: Extra depth in linear networks can implicitly precondition gradient descent and accelerate optimization without increasing expressiveness.

paragraphs: SMAC addresses collections of heterogeneous objects, such as images or three-dimensional shapes, for which some pairwise maps have already been computed. The task is to organize the objects into homogeneous groups while making the relationships among them consistent. The method treats grouping and map estimation as a joint problem.

Its input consists of the object collection and available maps between selected pairs. It produces both a clustering and a revised set of maps with optimal consistency within and between clusters. The method assembles pairwise maps as blocks of a data matrix and uses spectral decomposition of that matrix to carry out the joint analysis.

The authors provide tight theoretical guarantees for exactness under established noise models and demonstrate usefulness on synthetic and real datasets. The guarantees tie exact recovery to the modeled noise setting. The broader contribution is a single spectral approach that links which objects belong together with how their maps should agree, allowing those two aspects of structure to be resolved together.
icml-2018-smac-simultaneous-mapping-and-.tldr: SMAC jointly clusters heterogeneous objects and improves map consistency through spectral decomposition, with exactness guarantees under specified noise models.

paragraphs: This paper develops learnable filters for neural networks that operate directly on raw waveform signals. The filters are continuous time-frequency atoms: parameterized building blocks for processing a signal in terms of its temporal and frequency content. The goal is to make this front-end processing part of end-to-end learning.

The authors derive analytical filters from a function space defined by a chosen smoothness order and boundary conditions. These mathematical constraints shape the family of available filters. Because the resulting filters are differentiable, their parameters can be optimized with gradients, allowing them to be used with deep neural networks as a trainable front end.

The approach is applied to large-scale bird detection using the freefield1010 dataset. The stated challenges include raw inputs with more than 100,000 dimensions and additional noise from multiple sources and soundscapes. This application brings the filter construction into a demanding waveform-processing setting, demonstrating how an explicitly defined family of continuous filters can participate in neural-network training directly from raw signals.
icml-2018-spline-filters-for-end-to-end-.tldr: Differentiable spline-based time-frequency filters provide a trainable front end for neural networks processing raw waveforms.

paragraphs: Deep networks can generalize well even when their parameter counts exceed the number of training examples. This paper seeks stronger mathematical explanations of that behavior. It observes that earlier PAC-Bayes and margin-based analyses had not yet produced sample-complexity bounds better than simply counting parameters, and develops a compression-based framework instead.

The approach explicitly and efficiently compresses a trained network into a more succinct parameterization. That compact representation supports generalization bounds reported to be orders of magnitude better in practice. The mathematical explanation therefore depends on the trained network's capacity for compression, giving a role to properties that raw parameter counting does not capture.

To establish that the compression works, the authors identify noise-stability properties of trained networks and verify them experimentally. They also extend the study of these properties and the resulting bounds to convolutional networks. Alongside the improved guarantees, the analysis offers theoretical support for the empirical success of network compression by connecting stable trained behavior to a smaller effective description.
icml-2018-stronger-generalization-bounds.tldr: Efficient compression and noise-stability properties yield substantially stronger practical generalization bounds for trained deep networks.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes linear regression by measuring residuals with an Orlicz norm. Such a norm is defined through a nonnegative convex function G that vanishes at zero. The authors focus on functions G with subquadratic growth, giving a specified family of losses for which they develop efficient approximation methods.

Their main tool is an oblivious subspace embedding that maps the column space of an n-by-d matrix into a lower-dimensional space measured with the Euclidean norm. The guarantee holds for every vector in that column space. The embedded norm lies between an Omega(1/(d log n)) multiple and an O(d² log n) multiple of the original Orlicz norm.

This controlled distortion allows the authors to obtain an O(d log² n)-factor approximation for Orlicz-norm regression. The contribution is a reduction from a more general norm geometry to a smaller Euclidean representation with explicit guarantees. They also apply their techniques to improve an algorithm for low-rank matrix approximation under l_p losses when 1 ≤ p < 2.
icml-2018-subspace-embedding-and-linear-.tldr: A lower-dimensional Euclidean embedding enables provable approximation algorithms for regression with subquadratic Orlicz norms.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples produced by standard methods do not consistently fool classifiers after physical-world changes such as shifts in viewpoint or camera noise. This paper addresses that fragility by developing an algorithm to synthesize examples that remain adversarial across a chosen distribution of transformations. Robustness to those transformations becomes part of the generation objective.

The authors first synthesize two-dimensional adversarial images that withstand noise, distortion, and affine transformations. They then apply the algorithm to complex three-dimensional objects and manufacture physical examples using 3D printing. This carries the approach from transformed images into objects that can exist outside a purely digital image-processing pipeline.

The results demonstrate the existence of physical three-dimensional adversarial objects. The chosen transformation distribution is central to the claim: the method targets adversarial behavior across that distribution, rather than asserting success under every possible viewing condition. The contribution shows that natural transformations need not destroy an adversarial example when robustness to those changes is explicitly incorporated into its synthesis.
icml-2018-synthesizing-robust-adversaria.tldr: Optimizing adversarial examples across a chosen transformation distribution produces robust images and physical 3D-printed adversarial objects.

paragraphs: Training systems with several interacting losses, such as generative adversarial networks, introduces dynamics that differ from minimizing a single objective. This paper develops tools for understanding and controlling gradient-based learning in general differentiable games. Its starting point is that familiar convergence reasoning for single-objective optimization does not carry over directly to these interactions.

The key result decomposes second-order game dynamics into two components. One relates to potential games, whose behavior can be understood through gradient descent on an implicit function. The other relates to Hamiltonian games, introduced here as a class obeying a conservation law analogous to those in classical mechanics. This separates two distinct mathematical contributions to the learning dynamics.

The decomposition motivates Symplectic Gradient Adjustment, an algorithm intended to find stable fixed points in general games. Basic experiments show competitive performance against recent methods for finding local Nash equilibria in GANs. The authors also establish applicability and guarantees in more general games, connecting the dynamical analysis to an optimization method with scope beyond the experimental GAN setting.
icml-2018-the-mechanics-of-n-player-diff.tldr: Decomposing game dynamics into potential and Hamiltonian components motivates Symplectic Gradient Adjustment for finding stable fixed points.

paragraphs: This paper proposes Inherent Structure Capacity, or ISC, to study the representational capacity of restricted Boltzmann machines. Inspired by a formalism used for spin glasses, ISC measures the expected number of distribution modes produced by a fixed architecture when parameters are drawn from a prior. Capacity is therefore defined relative to this particular measure.

Although ISC is intractable to compute, the authors show that it approaches a finite constant as hidden units are added to a single-layer RBM. Improving ISC further requires a second layer. They introduce lean multilayer RBMs, in which each layer contains at most O(n) units for n visible units.

For every single-layer RBM with Omega(n^(2+r)) hidden units, where r is nonnegative, the authors establish the existence of a two-layer lean RBM with Theta(n²) parameters and the same ISC. This provides a quantitative advantage for layering under the proposed capacity measure: a substantially smaller two-layer architecture can match the ISC of a much wider single-layer model.
icml-2018-using-inherent-structures-to-d.tldr: Under Inherent Structure Capacity, lean two-layer RBMs can match much wider single-layer models using substantially fewer parameters.
